extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media watchdogs, researchers, and the general public concerned with media transparency
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and discussion for detecting when a published news article is essentially a press release (i.e., 'churnalism'), including a description, examples, technical detection approach used by churnalism.com, and recommended transparency practices for news outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of churnalism
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of ‘churnalism’ is a news article that is published as journalism, but is essentially a press release without much added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites Nick Davies' usage in Flat Earth News and frames churnalism as published material that is 'essentially a press release' rather than original reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources prone to producing churnalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Churnalism often originates from PR material produced by commercial companies, public authorities, medical firms, political lobbying groups, and other organized interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Travelodge survey releases, Migration Watch UK releases, corporate product promotions, and industry/retailer PR; both national and local papers rely heavily on such material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotional/agenda-driven nature as a criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: PR material is designed to promote or suppress stories in order to serve political, commercial or other groups' interests, and this promotional agenda is a central concern when assessing churnalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the material is not untrue, it is 'manufactured' to serve interests and becomes problematic when disguised as independent journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency requirement (link to press release)
rubrics_metrics.description: News outlets should be transparent about their sources by linking to the press release from the article so readers can judge agenda and origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given online publication and ease of linking, any news outlet could link to the press release; doing so would help readers evaluate the provenance and potential bias of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable uses of press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all press releases are bad: releases about major government announcements, medical breakthroughs, or matters clearly in the public interest can legitimately form the basis of news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rubric acknowledges that some press release-derived stories are appropriate and in the public interest; the concern is undisclosed reliance and lack of original reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of lazy journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs that an article is churnalism include copying text, quotes, images, and video from press releases; publishing without any sign the journalist conducted additional reporting (e.g., did not 'pick up the phone').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases often 'provide text, quotes, images, and sometimes even video footage' and 'the story quite literally writes itself' — absence of added reporting or verification is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative similarity threshold used to flag churn (>20%)
rubrics_metrics.description: Churnalism.com flags articles as possible churn if the similarity between a pasted press release and an article exceeds 20 percent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The site's churn engine compresses the input and searches for common hashes; if similarity is greater than 20% it 'suggests the article may be churn.' This is presented as a pragmatic heuristic rather than an absolute proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical detection method (compression, hashing, matching)
rubrics_metrics.description: The detection methodology compresses articles into numerical representations based on fifteen-character strings (via a hash function), stores them, and matches compressed forms to find common hashes between releases and articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors tried other methods (e.g., distinctive words) which were 'highly erratic,' and settled on a compression/re-indexing/matching approach backed by a database of over three million compressed articles from national press, BBC, and Sky News online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of simple word-matching
rubrics_metrics.description: Searching for distinctive words present in both the press release and news articles can be useful but proved 'highly erratic' and unreliable in pinpointing churn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This motivates using more robust compression/hashing techniques; practitioners should be cautious about equating shared vocabulary with churn without stronger matching criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evidence thresholds (examples of percent copied)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples show substantial verbatim reuse: in one case an article used 52% of a press release; other articles used 'only slightly less' or 'over a third' of releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These example percentages illustrate real-world reuse levels and help contextualize the 20% heuristic — high percentages serve as clear indicators of heavy reliance on PR text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and limits of detection tools (awareness, not cure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tools like churnalism.com are intended to provide a way for people to distinguish between journalism and churnalism and to raise awareness, but they are not a complete solution to the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The site 'is not going to “solve” the churnalism problem' — PR practices, agency feeds, and commercial relationships mean that copying will continue; the tool's role is to encourage transparency and better practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended journalist ethical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should think twice before putting their byline on copy that is largely press release text and should link to the press release when appropriate; they should add original reporting and verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bylines should not be used on work that is essentially the PR department's copy; adding sourcing transparency and original reporting helps readers evaluate trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical user workflow for detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Users can paste a press release into churnalism.com, click 'compare', and the engine will compare it against a corpus of national press, BBC, and Sky News articles to report percentages of cut-and-paste reuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The site leverages a fast-access database of compressed articles (from journalisted.com) and returns which news articles contain common hashes and what percentage of the press release was reused.
